prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire flat-band systems

statement.case_for: After reading the opening ballots I now put magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, ahead of my own opening choice, the geometric phases. It is the only shortlisted candidate with broad support across the table (seven of eight members rank it, five in their top three, two first). The scientific case is a rare, clean sequence: a parameter-free continuum-model prediction of flat bands at a magic angle (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011), then the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, then rapid independent reproduction across many moire platforms. A single geometric knob tunes strongly correlated matter, and the field has since produced new states (for example fractional Chern insulators in moire systems). The theory-plus-experiment shape fits the prize well, and the three credited names map onto the decisive prediction and the decisive experimental programme.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are timing and attribution. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity and the nature of several correlated states are still contested, so the field's conceptual resolution is incomplete, and I said in my opening that recognition may be somewhat early. On credit, the experimental first authors (Yuan Cao, Valla Fatemi) and other contributors (Dean, Young, Ashoori, and early theorists such as Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) fall outside the three supplied names, and a three-person limit forces a hard choice that this list resolves only imperfectly. If the committee judges that moire physics is still too young or that the credit is too contested, B061 is the more finished alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because nature delivered a new regime that a prediction anticipated, and he judges the discovery solid even though the pairing mechanism is unresolved; he also flags that other experimental groups may deserve credit.
responses.response: I agree that the discovery is secure and that unresolved pairing is a question about follow-on physics, not about the existence of the flat-band platform. That moves me off my earlier worry about prematurity. I would qualify one point: the credit worry is not only about other experimental groups. The first-author role of Cao and Fatemi cannot be represented under a three-name cap, so our citation should name the prediction and the observed phases, not any claim about who did all the experiments.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that this is a rare case where calculation anticipated a qualitatively new regime and experiment confirmed it, and he asks whether MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero alone could carry the prize, flagging earlier twisted-graphene theory by others.
responses.response: I share the view that the prediction-then-confirmation structure is the strongest argument. On Eriksson's two-name alternative I disagree: dropping Bistritzer would credit the continuum model to MacDonald alone, although the 2011 prediction is a joint paper with Bistritzer as first author, and I see no principled reason to remove him while keeping the other two. On the earlier work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, I accept it as real history, but the magic-angle flat-band condition is what the prediction identified, and that is the decisive step.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first because the magic-wavelength and blackbody-shift physics is directly judgeable, the result is strongly confirmed, and the 2005 comb prize left the clock application itself unrecognised.
responses.response: I take her atomic-physics judgement seriously, since I ranked B061 fifth mostly on maturity grounds and not on doubts about its quality, and I agree that it is the more finished result. Where I differ is on priority: the clocks are a precision refinement of a measurement tradition already honoured in 2005 and 2012, whereas moire quantum matter is a new regime of nature. I would not oppose B061 and have named it as my first alternative, but I do not accept that its maturity by itself outweighs the originality of the moire discovery.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first as a clean, concrete advance whose distinctness from the prior comb prize is clear, and notes the redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll that the two-name Katori and Ye configuration is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and that is a real advantage over twisted bilayer graphene. My reservation is that the pending redefinition of the second means the practical culmination is still ahead, while he calls it a decisive, lasting result. I think both statements can hold, but they do not make the clocks more novel than the moire platform, so we disagree on weighting, not on facts.

responses.point: Johansson ranks Cirac and Zoller first as the conceptual blueprint for physical quantum information processing, with a clean two-person credit, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene second.
responses.response: I ranked Cirac and Zoller sixth. The originality is not in doubt, but the proposal lineage is already partly recognised through the 2012 prize and the 2022 entanglement prize, and the citation would have to choose between trapped-ion gates and cold-atom simulation, which Johansson himself lists as an unresolved scope question. A theory-only prize for quantum information also sits less comfortably with the criterion that the discovery be one that nature delivered. I see the moire candidate as more clearly a new phenomenon and would therefore not put B034 ahead of it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a genuine invention, and she ranks twisted bilayer graphene fifth as probably slightly early, while proposing Hosono alone for iron-based superconductors.
responses.response: Her timing concern echoes my own opening ballot, and I now weigh it less because many independent groups have reproduced the phases and the platform has already generated new fields. I do not dispute the case for aberration correction as an invention with a large impact on how condensed-matter structure is measured, but the attribution risk she flags (Knut Urban omitted from the credited set) is of the same kind as the one I raise for moire, and a three-name cap makes it harder to defend. I am also unconvinced that a Hosono-only configuration is the cleanest credit for iron pnictides when Chen and Zhao drove the key Tc increase.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards moire quantum matter as mature enough, given the unsettled superconducting mechanism, or prefers to wait.
Whether the omission of Yuan Cao, Valla Fatemi and other experimental and theoretical contributors can be defended in a three-name configuration.
Whether my opening first choice, the Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phases, can attract any support beyond my own ballot, or is better treated as a long-run candidate.
Overlap with earlier prizes (2010 graphene, 2016 topological phases) may affect how colleagues frame the citation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the credited names for the shortlisted candidates appears among my documented co-authors or supervisors. My research (turbulent particles, random matrices, complex systems) is not close to moire materials or the other shortlisted fields, which I treat as a limit on my expertise, not a conflict.
